claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by voltage-clamp recordings showing in-phase inhibition in fast bifurcating V2a neurons (Figure 6).

claims.claim: At slow speeds recurrent inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing.
claims.source: In contrast, at slow speeds recurrent inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing, while bifurcating V2a neurons rely on reciprocal inhibition alone to pattern output.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by voltage-clamp recordings showing in-phase inhibition in slow descending V2a neurons (Figure 6).

claims.claim: At slow speeds bifurcating V2a neurons rely on reciprocal inhibition alone to pattern output.
claims.source: In contrast, at slow speeds recurrent inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing, while bifurcating V2a neurons rely on reciprocal inhibition alone to pattern output.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by voltage-clamp recordings showing predominantly anti-phase inhibition in slow bifurcating V2a neurons (Figure 6).

claims.claim: Cell-type-specific, not common, modes of rhythmogenesis generate and coordinate different speeds of locomotion.
claims.source: Our findings suggest cell-type-specific, not common, modes of rhythmogenesis generate and coordinate different speeds of locomotion.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing all experimental findings.

claims.claim: All forms of vertebrate locomotion rely on rhythmic activity in muscles operating as functional antagonists.
claims.source: All forms of vertebrate locomotion rely on rhythmic activity in muscles operating as functional antagonists (Grillner, 1985).
claims.evidence: This is a general statement supported by a citation to established literature.

claims.claim: Swimming in fishes relies on left–right alternation of axial muscles across the body.
claims.source: For instance, swimming in fishes relies on left–right alternation of axial muscles across the body, while walking in mammals relies on flexor–extensor alternation along it.
claims.evidence: This is a well-established fact about fish locomotion.

claims.claim: Walking in mammals relies on flexor–extensor alternation along the body.
claims.source: For instance, swimming in fishes relies on left–right alternation of axial muscles across the body, while walking in mammals relies on flexor–extensor alternation along it.
claims.evidence: This is a well-established fact about mammalian locomotion.

claims.claim: A landmark hypothesis posed over a century ago argued for corresponding excitatory 'half-centers' within spinal cord with reciprocal, feedforward inhibition between half-centers generating rhythmic output.
claims.source: A landmark hypothesis posed over a century ago argued for corresponding excitatory 'half-centers' within spinal cord (e.g., left–right or flexor–extensor), with reciprocal, feedforward inhibition between half-centers generating rhythmic output (Brown, 1911).
claims.evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citation to Brown, 1911.

claims.claim: Reciprocal inhibition has been relegated to patterning activity between so-called 'unit burst generators' capable of rhythmogenesis via recurrent, feedback excitatory connections.
claims.source: Since then reciprocal inhibition has been relegated to patterning activity between so-called 'unit burst generators' capable of rhythmogenesis via recurrent, feedback excitatory connections (Grillner and Kozlov, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about current theory supported by citation.

claims.claim: Simulations adjusting the synaptic coupling strength between segmental axial unit burst generators can explain changes in the speed and direction of swimming in lampreys.
claims.source: For example, simulations adjusting the synaptic coupling strength between segmental axial unit burst generators can explain changes in the speed and direction of swimming in lampreys (Kozlov et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to computational modeling work.

claims.claim: Simulations altering the synaptic coupling between segmental limb unit burst generators can replicate different speeds and gaits of locomotion in cats.
claims.source: Likewise, simulations altering the synaptic coupling between segmental limb unit burst generators can replicate different speeds and gaits of locomotion in cats (Grillner, 1981).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to computational modeling work.

claims.claim: Another theory explaining speed-dependent changes in coordination stratifies 'rhythm' and 'pattern' control.
claims.source: Another theory explaining speed-dependent changes in coordination stratifies 'rhythm' and 'pattern' control (Perret and Cabelguen, 1980; Koshland and Smith, 1989; Kriellaars et al., 1994; Burke et al., 2001; Lafreniere-Roula and McCrea, 2005), where populations of interneurons generating higher- or lower-frequency rhythms feed into separate populations coordinating distinct patterns of motor output (McCrea and Rybak, 2008; Ausborn et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical framework supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Studies in zebrafish and mice suggest separate spinal populations are active at different locomotor speeds with distinct patterns of motor output.
claims.source: In support, studies in zebrafish and mice suggest separate spinal populations are active at different locomotor speeds with distinct patterns of motor output (McLean et al., 2008; Talpalar et al., 2013; Satou et al., 2020; Picton et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Rhythmogenesis is presumed to originate from a common mechanism regardless of speed, reliant on cellular properties or synaptic drive or both.
claims.source: Critically, however, rhythmogenesis is presumed to originate from a common mechanism regardless of speed, reliant on cellular properties or synaptic drive or both (Guertin, 2009; Brocard et al., 2010; Ryczko et al., 2010; Ziskind-Conhaim and Hochman, 2017; El Manira, 2023).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about prevailing assumptions in the field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Larval zebrafish generate two basic modes of forward swimming or 'gaits'.
claims.source: Like all fish, larval zebrafish generate two basic modes of forward swimming or 'gaits' (Di Santo et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about zebrafish locomotion supported by citation.

claims.claim: Anguilliform mode is typically reserved for escaping predators and uses higher-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the trunk.
claims.source: Anguilliform mode is typically reserved for escaping predators and uses higher-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the trunk, while carangiform mode utilizes lower-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the tail for exploration and pursuing prey (Budick and O'Malley, 2000; Müller and van Leeuwen, 2004; Thorsen et al., 2004; Patterson et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of zebrafish swimming modes supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Carangiform mode utilizes lower-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the tail for exploration and pursuing prey.
claims.source: Anguilliform mode is typically reserved for escaping predators and uses higher-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the trunk, while carangiform mode utilizes lower-frequency/-amplitude oscillations of the tail for exploration and pursuing prey (Budick and O'Malley, 2000; Müller and van Leeuwen, 2004; Thorsen et al., 2004; Patterson et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of zebrafish swimming modes supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Swimming at different speeds is generated by axial motor neurons organized into fast, slow, and intermediate units distinguished by birth order.
claims.source: Swimming at different speeds is generated by axial motor neurons organized into fast, slow, and intermediate units distinguished by birth order (Myers et al., 1986), size (McLean et al., 2007), relative innervation of fast and slow muscle fibers (Bello-Rojas et al., 2019), and molecular signatures (D'Elia et al., 2023; Pallucchi et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing motor neuron properties.

claims.claim: Axial motor neurons are distinguished by size.
claims.source: Swimming at different speeds is generated by axial motor neurons organized into fast, slow, and intermediate units distinguished by birth order (Myers et al., 1986), size (McLean et al., 2007), relative innervation of fast and slow muscle fibers (Bello-Rojas et al., 2019), and molecular signatures (D'Elia et al., 2023; Pallucchi et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to McLean et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Axial motor neurons are distinguished by relative innervation of fast and slow muscle fibers.
claims.source: Swimming at different speeds is generated by axial motor neurons organized into fast, slow, and intermediate units distinguished by birth order (Myers et al., 1986), size (McLean et al., 2007), relative innervation of fast and slow muscle fibers (Bello-Rojas et al., 2019), and molecular signatures (D'Elia et al., 2023; Pallucchi et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Bello-Rojas et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Axial motor neurons are distinguished by molecular signatures.
claims.source: Swimming at different speeds is generated by axial motor neurons organized into fast, slow, and intermediate units distinguished by birth order (Myers et al., 1986), size (McLean et al., 2007), relative innervation of fast and slow muscle fibers (Bello-Rojas et al., 2019), and molecular signatures (D'Elia et al., 2023; Pallucchi et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to D'Elia et al., 2023 and Pallucchi et al., 2024.

claims.claim: Current- and voltage-clamp recordings from motor neurons have revealed differences in rhythmogenic cellular properties and synaptic drive between the different types.
claims.source: Current- and voltage-clamp recordings from motor neurons have revealed differences in rhythmogenic cellular properties and synaptic drive between the different types (Menelaou and McLean, 2012; Kishore et al., 2014), suggesting different forms of rhythmogenesis could be responsible for different speeds of locomotion.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the same lab.

claims.claim: Chx10-labeled spinal V2a interneurons provide a major source of phasic premotor excitation during locomotion in zebrafish and mice.
claims.source: To test this idea, we performed current- and voltage-clamp recordings from Chx10-labeled spinal V2a interneurons, which provide a major source of phasic premotor excitation during locomotion in zebrafish and mice (McLean and Dougherty, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claims.claim: Morphologically distinct V2a neurons sort into rhythm-generating and pattern-forming subtypes based on distinct cellular properties linked to distinct patterns of recruitment and synaptic drive.
claims.source: We find that morphologically distinct V2a neurons sort into rhythm-generating and pattern-forming subtypes based on distinct cellular properties linked to distinct patterns of recruitment and synaptic drive.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings stated in the Introduction and supported by data in Figures 2-6.

claims.claim: Among descending V2a neurons that qualify as rhythm-generating, reciprocal inhibition originating from contralateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at fast speeds.
claims.source: Critically, among descending V2a neurons that qualify as rhythm-generating, reciprocal inhibition originating from contralateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at fast speeds, while recurrent inhibition from ipsilateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at slow speeds.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Among descending V2a neurons that qualify as rhythm-generating, recurrent inhibition from ipsilateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at slow speeds.
claims.source: Critically, among descending V2a neurons that qualify as rhythm-generating, reciprocal inhibition originating from contralateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at fast speeds, while recurrent inhibition from ipsilateral sources supports phasic firing patterns at slow speeds.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: For bifurcating V2a neurons considered pattern-forming, recurrent inhibition supports phasic firing at fast speeds.
claims.source: For bifurcating V2a neurons considered pattern-forming, the opposite is true – recurrent inhibition supports phasic firing at fast speeds and reciprocal inhibition at slow speeds.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: For bifurcating V2a neurons considered pattern-forming, reciprocal inhibition supports phasic firing at slow speeds.
claims.source: For bifurcating V2a neurons considered pattern-forming, the opposite is true – recurrent inhibition supports phasic firing at fast speeds and reciprocal inhibition at slow speeds.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: V2a neurons are organized into fast and slow subtypes based on dorsoventral (DV) soma position and birth order.
claims.source: From our previous work studying V2a neurons in larval zebrafish we know they are organized into: (1) fast and slow subtypes based on dorsoventral (DV) soma position and birth order (McLean et al., 2007; McLean et al., 2008; McLean and Fetcho, 2009), and (2) distinct subtypes that provide stronger direct versus indirect control of motor neuron recruitment (Menelaou et al., 2014; Menelaou and McLean, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work from the same lab.

claims.claim: V2a neurons with descending axons (V2a-D) provide stronger inputs to other premotor interneurons.
claims.source: Specifically, V2a neurons with descending axons (V2a-D) provide stronger inputs to other premotor interneurons, while V2a neurons with bifurcating axons (V2a-B) provide stronger inputs to motor neurons (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), in line with differential rhythm and pattern control.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: V2a neurons with bifurcating axons (V2a-B) provide stronger inputs to motor neurons.
claims.source: Specifically, V2a neurons with descending axons (V2a-D) provide stronger inputs to other premotor interneurons, while V2a neurons with bifurcating axons (V2a-B) provide stronger inputs to motor neurons (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), in line with differential rhythm and pattern control.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Midbody V2a neurons would be recruited during both fast anguilliform and slow carangiform modes.
claims.source: To record from distinct types of V2a neurons, we targeted green fluorescent protein (GFP)-positive neurons located at midbody in the Tg(Chx10:GFP) line (Figure 1A, B; Kimura et al., 2006), since midbody neurons would be recruited during both fast anguilliform and slow carangiform modes (Müller and van Leeuwen, 2004; Thorsen et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of zebrafish swimming.

claims.claim: V2a-D and V2a-B neurons recruited at fast speeds can be distinguished by levels of Chx10 expression in transgenic lines.
claims.source: V2a-D and V2a-B neurons recruited at fast speeds can be distinguished by levels of Chx10 expression in transgenic lines (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), as reported in mice (Hayashi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in zebrafish and mice.

claims.claim: Larger, dimmer V2a neurons intermingled with smaller, brighter neurons along the DV axis.
claims.source: Larger, dimmer V2a neurons intermingled with smaller, brighter neurons along the DV axis (Figure 1C, left), but occupied more lateral positions (Figure 1C, right).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Larger, dimmer V2a neurons occupied more lateral positions than smaller, brighter neurons.
claims.source: Larger, dimmer V2a neurons intermingled with smaller, brighter neurons along the DV axis (Figure 1C, left), but occupied more lateral positions (Figure 1C, right).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference in DV distribution between low and high GFP-positive V2a neuron types.
claims.source: Statistical analysis confirmed these observations, with no significant difference in either DV distribution (Figure 1D, left) or number per segment between the low or high GFP-positive types (Figure 1D, right), but a significant difference in ML position (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D with statistical test results.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference in number per segment between low and high GFP-positive V2a neuron types.
claims.source: Statistical analysis confirmed these observations, with no significant difference in either DV distribution (Figure 1D, left) or number per segment between the low or high GFP-positive types (Figure 1D, right), but a significant difference in ML position (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D with statistical test results.

claims.claim: There is a significant difference in ML position between low and high GFP-positive V2a neuron types.
claims.source: Statistical analysis confirmed these observations, with no significant difference in either DV distribution (Figure 1D, left) or number per segment between the low or high GFP-positive types (Figure 1D, right), but a significant difference in ML position (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E with statistical test results.

claims.claim: During real swimming escape responses decelerate, beginning in fast anguilliform mode and ending in slow carangiform mode.
claims.source: During real swimming escape responses decelerate (Video 1), beginning in fast anguilliform mode and ending in slow carangiform mode (McLean et al., 2008; McLean and Fetcho, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text, supported by citations, and illustrated in Video 1.

claims.claim: Plots of ventral rootlet burst frequencies with time confirm the deceleration pattern during 'fictive' escape responses.
claims.source: Plots of ventral rootlet burst frequencies with time confirm this pattern during 'fictive' escape responses, where we observe the highest frequencies at the beginning of the swim episode immediately following the stimulus (Figure 1G, left).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Zebrafish swimming is episodic.
claims.source: Notably, zebrafish swimming is episodic (McHenry and Lauder, 2006; Soto and McHenry, 2020) and so it can continue intermittently after the initial escape swim episode.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Subsequent swim episodes (Swim 2+) rarely exceeded peak firing frequencies observed in the first stimulus-evoked episode (>60 Hz in Swim 1).
claims.source: Subsequent episodes (Swim 2+) rarely exceeded peak firing frequencies observed in the first stimulus-evoked episode (>60 Hz in Swim 1) and there was more variability in frequency (Figure 1G, right).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: All high GFP neurons targeted for recordings were V2a-Ds.
claims.source: By including dye in our recording pipette, we confirmed post hoc that all high GFP neurons we targeted for recordings were V2a-Ds and all low GFP neurons were V2a-Bs (Figure 2A), as we would expect based on our prior work (Menelaou and McLean, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2A, and supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: All low GFP neurons targeted for recordings were V2a-Bs.
claims.source: By including dye in our recording pipette, we confirmed post hoc that all high GFP neurons we targeted for recordings were V2a-Ds and all low GFP neurons were V2a-Bs (Figure 2A), as we would expect based on our prior work (Menelaou and McLean, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figure 2A, and supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Differences in sizes and DV distributions of V2a-D and V2a-B neurons in the current-clamp dataset were consistent with analysis of high and low GFP neurons in stable lines.
claims.source: Differences in sizes and DV distributions of V2a-D and V2a-B neurons in our current-clamp dataset (n = 47) were consistent with our analysis of high and low GFP neurons in stable lines (Figure 2B, left).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Measurements of input resistance and rheobase current were consistent with differences in sizes and excitability between V2a-D and V2a-B types.
claims.source: Also, measurements of input resistance and rheobase current were consistent with differences in sizes and excitability between the two types (Figure 2C, left).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: V2a-D neurons with 'tonic' responses were distributed dorsally and had the lowest input resistances in their respective types.
claims.source: V2a-D neurons with 'tonic' responses and V2a-B neurons with higher-frequency 'chattering' ones were distributed dorsally and had the lowest input resistances in their respective types (Figure 2B–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2B-E.

claims.claim: V2a-B neurons with higher-frequency 'chattering' responses were distributed dorsally and had the lowest input resistances in their respective types.
claims.source: V2a-D neurons with 'tonic' responses and V2a-B neurons with higher-frequency 'chattering' ones were distributed dorsally and had the lowest input resistances in their respective types (Figure 2B–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2B-E.

claims.claim: In tonic V2a-Ds, firing above rheobase current was observed consistently throughout the current step.
claims.source: In tonic V2a-Ds, firing above rheobase current was observed consistently throughout the current step (Figure 2E, top), with instantaneous spike rates increasing linearly with increasing current, starting around 40 Hz and reaching 200 Hz (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: In tonic V2a-Ds, instantaneous spike rates increased linearly with increasing current, starting around 40 Hz and reaching 200 Hz.
claims.source: In tonic V2a-Ds, firing above rheobase current was observed consistently throughout the current step (Figure 2E, top), with instantaneous spike rates increasing linearly with increasing current, starting around 40 Hz and reaching 200 Hz (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: In chattering V2a-Bs, firing above rheobase current was intermittent throughout the step.
claims.source: In chattering V2a-Bs, firing above rheobase current was intermittent throughout the step (Figure 2F, top), with instantaneous rates starting around 200 Hz and reaching 600 Hz (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2D and 2F.

claims.claim: In chattering V2a-Bs, instantaneous rates started around 200 Hz and reached 600 Hz.
claims.source: In chattering V2a-Bs, firing above rheobase current was intermittent throughout the step (Figure 2F, top), with instantaneous rates starting around 200 Hz and reaching 600 Hz (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Observations of tonic V2a-D and chattering V2a-B firing patterns are consistent with previous recordings from fast V2a-D and V2a-B neurons.
claims.source: These observations are consistent with previous recordings from fast V2a-D and V2a-B neurons (Menelaou and McLean, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: V2a-D and V2a-B neurons with 'burst' responses were distributed ventrally and had the highest input resistances within their respective types.
claims.source: On the other hand, V2a-D and V2a-B neurons with 'burst' responses were distributed ventrally and had the highest input resistances within their respective types (Figure 2B–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2B-E.

claims.claim: In bursting V2a neurons, firing above rheobase was characterized by higher-frequency spikes superimposed on lower-frequency membrane potential oscillations.
claims.source: In bursting V2a neurons, firing above rheobase was characterized by higher-frequency spikes superimposed on lower-frequency membrane potential oscillations (Figure 2E, F, bottom).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claims.claim: The frequency of the slower oscillations in bursting V2a neurons increased with current.
claims.source: While the frequency of the slower oscillations increased with current (Figure 2E, F, bottom), instantaneous spike rates were already close to peak values at rheobase (500–600 Hz; Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2D, 2E, and 2F.

claims.claim: Instantaneous spike rates in bursting V2a neurons were already close to peak values at rheobase (500–600 Hz).
claims.source: While the frequency of the slower oscillations increased with current (Figure 2E, F, bottom), instantaneous spike rates were already close to peak values at rheobase (500–600 Hz; Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Beyond 2–3x rheobase current, slower oscillations in bursting V2a neurons were no longer obvious and the firing pattern more closely resembled the chattering one.
claims.source: Beyond 2–3x rheobase current, slower oscillations were no longer obvious and the firing pattern more closely resembled the chattering one (data not shown), as observed previously for motor neurons (Menelaou and McLean, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to prior work on motor neurons.

claims.claim: Tonic V2a-D and chattering V2a-B neurons were recruited at the beginning of the episode at median swim frequencies above 30 Hz.
claims.source: As expected (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), both tonic V2a-D and chattering V2a-B neurons were recruited at the beginning of the episode at median swim frequencies above 30 Hz (Figure 2G, H), consistent with recruitment during fast anguilliform mode (Thorsen et al., 2004; McLean et al., 2008; McLean and Fetcho, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figures 2G and 2H, and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Burst V2a-Ds fired more reliably at the end of the episode at median frequencies that rarely exceeded 30 Hz.
claims.source: In contrast, burst V2a-Ds fired more reliably at the end of the episode at median frequencies that rarely exceeded 30 Hz (Figure 2G, H), consistent with participation in slow carangiform mode (Thorsen et al., 2004; McLean et al., 2008; McLean and Fetcho, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figures 2G and 2H, and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Burst V2a-Bs were recruited just below 30 Hz, and fired more reliably throughout the episode and over a broader frequency range.
claims.source: Burst V2a-Bs were recruited just below 30 Hz, and fired more reliably throughout the episode and over a broader frequency range (Figure 2G, H), particularly compared to the narrow range of bursting V2a-Ds (two sample Kolmogrov–Smirnov test on density distributions; D = 0.157, p < 0.001; BB, n = 6, BD, n = 8).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text, shown in Figures 2G and 2H, and supported by statistical analysis.

claims.claim: A comparison between the step- and swim-firing patterns among V2a-D neurons revealed a remarkable correspondence.
claims.source: A comparison between the step- and swim-firing patterns among V2a-D neurons revealed a remarkable correspondence (Figure 2G), with median spike frequencies (tonic) or oscillation frequencies (burst) overlapping median recruitment frequencies during swimming (Figure 2I, left).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2G and 2I.

claims.claim: Median spike frequencies (tonic) or oscillation frequencies (burst) in V2a-D neurons overlap median recruitment frequencies during swimming.
claims.source: A comparison between the step- and swim-firing patterns among V2a-D neurons revealed a remarkable correspondence (Figure 2G), with median spike frequencies (tonic) or oscillation frequencies (burst) overlapping median recruitment frequencies during swimming (Figure 2I, left).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: The link between step- and swim-firing patterns was less obvious for V2a-B neurons.
claims.source: However, the link between step- and swim-firing patterns was less obvious for V2a-B neurons (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: While bursting V2a-B neurons recruited at swim frequencies exceeding 60 Hz had higher-frequency oscillations, step bursting rarely exceeded 20 Hz.
claims.source: For example, while bursting V2a-B neurons recruited at swim frequencies exceeding 60 Hz had higher-frequency oscillations, step bursting rarely exceeded 20 Hz (Figure 2I, right).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: For chattering V2a-B neurons, there were no clear subthreshold oscillations to calculate rhythmicity.
claims.source: For chattering V2a-B neurons, there were no clear subthreshold oscillations to calculate rhythmicity and the broad range of spike frequencies resulted in large standard deviations (±74–130 Hz, n = 5) that rendered median values less interpretable.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text describing the analysis of chattering V2a-B neurons.

claims.claim: Distinct electrophysiological properties define distinct V2a types recruited at different speeds.
claims.source: Thus, distinct electrophysiological properties define distinct V2a types recruited at different speeds and V2a-D neurons are better suited to providing intrinsic rhythmogenic activity during fast and slow swimming modes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the current-clamp data presented.

claims.claim: V2a-D neurons are better suited to providing intrinsic rhythmogenic activity during fast and slow swimming modes.
claims.source: Thus, distinct electrophysiological properties define distinct V2a types recruited at different speeds and V2a-D neurons are better suited to providing intrinsic rhythmogenic activity during fast and slow swimming modes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the current-clamp data showing correspondence between intrinsic and swim firing patterns in V2a-D neurons.

claims.claim: V2a-B neurons rely more on rhythmic synaptic drive to shape their phasic firing patterns during swimming.
claims.source: This is consistent with their proposed rhythm-generating and pattern-forming roles (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), and suggests V2a-B neurons rely more on rhythmic synaptic drive to shape their phasic firing patterns during swimming.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correspondence between step- and swim-firing patterns in V2a-B neurons.

claims.claim: V2a-D and V2a-B neurons that fired at the beginning of the escape episode or nearer the end were found in the voltage-clamp dataset.
claims.source: Consistent with our current-clamp recordings, in our voltage-clamp dataset (n = 39) we found V2a-D and V2a-B neurons that fired at the beginning of the escape episode or nearer the end (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: V2a-D neurons fired more sparsely than V2a-B neurons.
claims.source: V2a-D neurons fired more sparsely (Figure 3A, left) and were divided into two distinct groups: (1) neurons that fired exclusively at the beginning of the episode at median swim frequencies exceeding 40 Hz, and (2) neurons that fired later on in the episode at median swim frequencies rarely exceeding 30 Hz (Figure 3B, top and bottom left; Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: V2a-D neurons were divided into two distinct groups based on firing timing and frequency.
claims.source: V2a-D neurons fired more sparsely (Figure 3A, left) and were divided into two distinct groups: (1) neurons that fired exclusively at the beginning of the episode at median swim frequencies exceeding 40 Hz, and (2) neurons that fired later on in the episode at median swim frequencies rarely exceeding 30 Hz (Figure 3B, top and bottom left; Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: V2a-B neurons fired more reliably than V2a-D neurons.
claims.source: On the other hand, V2a-B neurons fired more reliably (Figure 3A, right) and median values were more continuous, making it more difficult to group neurons based on location within the episode (Figure 3B, top and bottom right) or swim frequency (Figure 3D).

results.result: V2a neurons in larval zebrafish are divided into at least two morphological subtypes (descending V2a-D and bifurcating V2a-B) that can be distinguished by GFP expression levels, soma size, and mediolateral (ML) position in the spinal cord. High GFP neurons are V2a-Ds and low GFP neurons are V2a-Bs, with V2a-Ds occupying more lateral positions despite similar dorsoventral distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 and C49-C51 provide converging anatomical and imaging evidence from confocal microscopy and post-hoc fills that consistently demonstrate morphological differences between V2a subtypes. Statistical analyses confirm significant differences in ML position (C44) while showing no significant differences in DV distribution (C42) or number per segment (C43), supporting the anatomical characterization.

results.result: Descending V2a-D neurons exhibit intrinsic cellular properties suitable for rhythmogenesis at the speeds where they are recruited. Tonic V2a-Ds recruited at fast speeds (>30 Hz) show tonic firing at 40-200 Hz, while bursting V2a-Ds recruited at slow speeds (<30 Hz) show bursting at those frequencies. The correspondence between step-firing and swim-firing patterns is remarkable for V2a-Ds but less obvious for V2a-B neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C69 provide extensive current-clamp data showing that intrinsic firing properties of V2a-D neurons match their recruitment frequencies during swimming (C68-C69), with statistical correlations supporting this correspondence. The data demonstrate that V2a-D neurons possess rhythmogenic properties appropriate for their recruitment speeds, while V2a-B neurons lack this correspondence (C70-C71), supporting distinct functional roles.

results.result: Bifurcating V2a-B neurons are recruited more reliably across all speeds compared to V2a-D neurons, which fire more sparsely and in a stricter modular fashion. Fast V2a-B neurons reach 100% recruitment reliability above 35 Hz, while slow V2a-B neurons maintain 100% reliability below 35 Hz. V2a-D neurons show maximum 50% recruitment reliability in their respective speed ranges.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C87 provide cell-attached and voltage-clamp recordings demonstrating clear differences in recruitment patterns between V2a-D and V2a-B neurons across frequency ranges. Statistical analyses (C84-C87) confirm significant differences in recruitment probability, with V2a-B neurons firing significantly more spikes per burst (C93). The data consistently support the pattern-forming role of V2a-B neurons downstream of rhythmogenic V2a-D neurons.

results.result: At fast speeds, reciprocal (anti-phase) inhibition in descending V2a-D neurons supports phasic firing and rhythmogenesis, while recurrent (in-phase) inhibition in bifurcating V2a-B neurons helps pattern motor output. Fast V2a-Ds receive broadly distributed phasic inhibition with anti-phase peaks, while fast V2a-Bs receive both in-phase and anti-phase inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C120 provide voltage-clamp recordings showing distinct patterns of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents at fast speeds. The phase analysis (C111-C117) demonstrates that fast V2a-Ds receive predominantly reciprocal inhibition while fast V2a-Bs receive both reciprocal and recurrent inhibition. The timing and amplitude of synaptic currents (C99-C106) support the proposed functional roles, with maximum inhibition orders of magnitude larger than excitation, emphasizing the critical role of inhibition timing.

results.result: At slow speeds, recurrent (in-phase) inhibition in descending V2a-D neurons supports phasic firing and rhythmogenesis, while bifurcating V2a-B neurons rely predominantly on reciprocal (anti-phase) inhibition to pattern output. Slow V2a-Ds show two clear peaks in phasic inhibition (in-phase and anti-phase), while slow V2a-Bs receive predominantly anti-phase inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 and C116-C121 provide voltage-clamp data showing that the dominant mode of inhibition is flipped at slow speeds compared to fast speeds. The phase analysis demonstrates coherent peaks in both reciprocal and recurrent inhibition for slow V2a-Ds at slow speeds (C121), while slow V2a-Bs receive predominantly reciprocal inhibition (C118). This cell-type-specific and speed-dependent pattern of inhibition is well-documented across multiple neurons.

results.result: Synaptic silencing of commissural dI6 neurons using botulinum toxin disrupts rhythmogenesis at fast speeds (causing synchronous bilateral activity) but primarily affects motor output patterning at slow speeds (increasing burst duration and duty cycle without affecting frequency or phase). This supports the conclusion that reciprocal inhibition plays a dominant role in rhythm generation at fast speeds and pattern formation at slow speeds.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C142 provide genetic silencing experiments with clear phenotypic outcomes. The data show that dI6 silencing causes loss of left-right alternation at high frequencies (C132-C134) but maintains normal frequency and phase at low frequencies while increasing duty cycle (C137-C139). The differential effects at fast versus slow speeds (C136, C141) support the proposed speed-dependent roles of reciprocal inhibition. The inference that reciprocal inhibition near the hindbrain/spinal cord is essential for high-frequency rhythms (C161) is reasonable given the comparison to prior ablation studies.

results.result: Cell-type-specific, not common, modes of rhythmogenesis generate and coordinate different speeds of locomotion. All V2a neurons rely on phasic excitation and inhibition to sculpt rhythmic firing, but the specific patterns of synaptic drive vary by cell type and speed in a manner consistent with hierarchical organization and speed modularity.
results.evaluation: This is the main conclusion synthesizing all experimental findings. Claims C123-C126 provide interpretations of the phase analysis data showing that V2a-D neurons receive excitation earlier than V2a-B neurons (supporting hierarchical organization), and that the coherence of synaptic drive at different frequencies supports speed modularity. The conclusion that common mechanisms are insufficient (C184) is well-supported by the extensive evidence of cell-type-specific and speed-dependent differences in both intrinsic properties and synaptic drive patterns.

results.result: Prior work has established that V2a neurons are organized into fast/slow subtypes based on DV position and birth order, with V2a-D neurons providing stronger inputs to premotor interneurons and V2a-B neurons providing stronger inputs to motor neurons. Fast V2a-D neurons have longer intersegmental axons and form stronger connections with other V2a neurons, while V2a-B neurons have faster membrane time constants and more reliable motor neuron connections.
results.evaluation: These claims (C35-C39, C147-C151) summarize prior work from the same laboratory and are appropriately cited. The citations appear accurate and the characterizations are consistent with the referenced studies. This prior work provides essential context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: During fictive escape swimming evoked by electrical stimulation, zebrafish show a deceleration pattern with highest frequencies (>60 Hz) at the beginning of the first swim episode (Swim 1), followed by lower and more variable frequencies in subsequent episodes (Swim 2+). This pattern mirrors real swimming behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 describe the basic swimming behavior used throughout the study. The deceleration pattern is documented in ventral rootlet recordings (C46) and supported by prior citations (C45, C47). This establishes the experimental paradigm for all subsequent recordings.

results.result: V2a neurons show properties consistent with their proposed roles: median spike distributions occur in advance of motor burst centers (as expected for premotor excitatory interneurons), V2a-B neurons fire slightly before V2a-Ds (consistent with size-related time constants), and spike rates during swimming (200-600 Hz) overlap with rates observed during current steps at 1-2x rheobase.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C92 provide supporting evidence linking intrinsic properties to functional recruitment. The spike timing data (C82-C83) and spike rate comparisons (C88-C91) are well-documented and support the functional relevance of the current-clamp measurements. The observation that spike numbers decrease at higher frequencies (C92) is explained by shorter cycle periods.

results.result: Peak excitatory and inhibitory drive to V2a neurons is normalized to cellular excitability, with lower resistance neurons receiving orders of magnitude more current than higher resistance neurons. Maximum inhibition is orders of magnitude larger than maximum excitation, suggesting that the timing of inhibition plays a critical role in shaping rhythmic output.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C104 and C109 demonstrate significant negative correlations between maximum current and input resistance for both excitation and inhibition. The observation that inhibition greatly exceeds excitation (C109) is well-documented and leads to the reasonable inference that inhibition timing is critical (C110). This normalization to excitability is consistent with prior work (C101).

results.result: The timing of phasic excitation is consistent with hierarchical organization of V2a neurons (V2a-Ds upstream of V2a-Bs), and the presence of in-phase inhibition is associated with more coherent spike distributions in slow V2a-Ds and fast V2a-Bs.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 show that V2a-D neurons receive excitation earlier than V2a-B neurons, supporting hierarchical organization. Claim C119 links in-phase inhibition to spike coherence. These are reasonable interpretations of the phase distribution data, though they represent inferences rather than direct demonstrations of causality.

results.result: The initial hypothesis was that cellular properties would be more important for rhythmogenesis at slow speeds while synaptic drive would dominate at fast speeds. However, the findings show that phasic firing in both V2a-Ds and V2a-Bs is best explained by phasic patterns of synaptic excitation and inhibition, suggesting rhythms are generated by more rostral V2a-Ds where rhythmic excitation originates.
results.evaluation: Claim C152 states the initial hypothesis based on prior motor neuron work. Claims C153-C154 document the intrinsic properties of V2a-D neurons. Claim C155 presents the surprising finding that synaptic drive is critical for all V2a neurons. The inference that rhythms originate rostrally (C156) is reasonable given that phasic excitation is already rhythmic when it arrives at midbody neurons. This is supported by prior optogenetic and lesion studies (C157-C158).

results.result: The current synaptic silencing strategy included dI6 neurons extending into the hindbrain, unlike prior ablation studies that were limited to spinal dI6 neurons. This difference may explain why the current study shows disruption of fast swimming while prior ablation studies did not.
results.evaluation: Claim C159 accurately cites prior work showing that spinal dI6 ablation does not prevent fast swimming. Claim C160 documents that the current strategy included hindbrain dI6 neurons. This comparison is appropriate and helps explain the different outcomes, though the authors acknowledge other potential differences between ablation and silencing approaches.

results.result: The proposed model suggests that slow and fast modules have mirror-image wiring diagrams with type I V2a-D neurons providing rhythmogenesis and type II V2a-B neurons providing pattern formation. In the fast module, rhythmogenesis relies on reciprocal inhibition while recurrent inhibition limits motor output. In the slow module, recurrent inhibition supports rhythmogenesis in V2a-Ds while reciprocal inhibition patterns activity in V2a-Bs.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C175 present a comprehensive model integrating all experimental findings. The model is well-supported by the data showing cell-type-specific and speed-dependent patterns of inhibition. The citations to prior work in lampreys and frogs (C169-C171) appropriately contextualize the findings. The model represents a reasonable synthesis of the experimental evidence, though it remains a proposed framework requiring further testing.

results.result: Background claims about vertebrate locomotion, historical theories of rhythmogenesis, zebrafish swimming modes, motor neuron organization, and comparisons to other systems and life stages provide context for the current findings.
results.evaluation: These claims (C11-C29, C140, C143-C146, C176-C183) provide background information and context, all appropriately cited. The characterizations of prior work and general principles appear accurate. These claims establish the scientific context but do not represent novel findings from the current study.

results.result: Spinal motor neurons exhibit a range of rhythmogenic cellular properties that likely contribute to the higher-frequency bursts observed unilaterally during dI6 silencing experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C135 cites prior work showing that motor neurons have rhythmogenic properties. This is used to explain the observation of unilateral high-frequency bursting during bilateral synchrony in dI6 BoTx-GFP fish. The explanation is reasonable and appropriately cited.

results.result: V2a neurons in the Chx10:GFP line are divided into two populations based on GFP intensity and mediolateral (ML) position. Larger, dimmer (low GFP) V2a neurons occupy more lateral positions than smaller, brighter (high GFP) neurons, with no significant difference in dorsoventral (DV) distribution or number per segment between the two types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge these anatomical distinctions. Reviewer 1 states that 'bifurcating V2as are located more laterally in the spinal cord' and 'descending V2as display strong GFP labeling, while bifurcating V2as display weak GFP labeling.' The data in Figure 1C-E are accepted without critique.

results.result: Post-hoc morphological identification confirmed that high GFP neurons are V2a-Ds (descending) and low GFP neurons are V2a-Bs (bifurcating). V2a-D and V2a-B neurons differ in size, dorsoventral distribution, input resistance, and rheobase current, with tonic and chattering subtypes distributed dorsally and bursting subtypes distributed ventrally within each morphological type.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these characterizations without objection. Reviewer 1 notes 'these two cell types have different electrophysiological properties as revealed by patch-clamp recordings' and describes the morphological and electrophysiological distinctions in detail. Reviewer 3 praises the 'rigorous approach' where 'many parameters, including projection pattern, intracellular properties...were obtained from the same neuron.'

results.result: Current-clamp recordings reveal distinct intrinsic firing properties in V2a subtypes. Tonic V2a-Ds fire consistently throughout current steps with spike rates increasing linearly from ~40 to 200 Hz. Chattering V2a-Bs fire intermittently with rates from ~200 to 600 Hz. Bursting V2a neurons (both D and B) show higher-frequency spikes superimposed on lower-frequency membrane oscillations, with oscillation frequency increasing with current while spike rates remain near peak values at rheobase (500-600 Hz).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accept these electrophysiological characterizations. Reviewer 1 states 'positive current steps indicated that descending V2as comprise tonic spiking or bursting neurons. Bifurcating V2as comprise chattering or bursting neurons.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'cleverly used standard electrophysiological tests and analysis to tease out different neuronal properties' and that 'spike rates measured with current steps are physiologically relevant.'

results.result: V2a subtypes show distinct speed-dependent recruitment patterns during fictive swimming. Tonic V2a-D and chattering V2a-B neurons are recruited at fast speeds (>30 Hz), while burst V2a-Ds are recruited at slow speeds (<30 Hz). Burst V2a-Bs are recruited across a broader frequency range. Critically, for V2a-D neurons, intrinsic firing frequencies during current steps match their swim recruitment frequencies, suggesting they are suited for rhythmogenesis. In contrast, V2a-B neurons show poor correspondence between step and swim firing patterns, suggesting they rely more on synaptic drive.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support these findings. Reviewer 1 states 'descending tonic and bifurcating chattering neurons are recruited at the beginning of the swimming bout, at fast speeds...descending bursting neurons were preferentially recruited at the end of swimming bouts, at low speeds.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes that 'identification of V2a subtype is based directly on their recruitment at different locomotor speeds' and praises the comparison showing 'spike rates measured with current steps are physiologically relevant and observed during natural recruitment' (Figures 2 and 4).

results.result: Voltage-clamp recordings during fictive swimming reveal that V2a-D neurons fire sparsely and are divided into distinct fast (>35 Hz) and slow (<35 Hz) groups with exclusive recruitment at their respective speeds. V2a-B neurons fire more reliably across a broader frequency range. Fast V2a-D neurons reach ~50% recruitment reliability above 35 Hz, while slow V2a-D neurons rarely fire above 35 Hz. V2a-B neurons show higher recruitment probabilities, reaching 100% reliability. Spike rates during swimming (200-600 Hz) overlap with those during current steps at 1-2x rheobase. V2a-B neurons fire significantly more spikes per burst than V2a-Ds, consistent with their pattern-forming role downstream of rhythmic signals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these recruitment patterns and their functional implications. Reviewer 1 describes the recruitment differences in detail and notes 'the two types of V2a neurons display different recruitment patterns as a function of speed.' Reviewer 2 highlights that 'identification of V2a subtype is based directly on their recruitment at different locomotor speeds' and that the authors 'make comparisons of V2a spiking with current steps and during fictive swims' demonstrating physiological relevance.

results.result: Voltage-clamp analysis of synaptic drive reveals that fast V2a-Ds receive compound EPSCs during high-frequency swimming, while slow V2a-Ds receive EPSCs during slower swimming, consistent with their recruitment patterns. V2a-Bs receive EPSCs over a broader frequency range. Maximum excitatory and inhibitory currents show significant negative correlations with input resistance, indicating that peak synaptic drive is normalized to cellular excitability. For fast V2a neurons, both excitation and inhibition increase with frequency. For slow V2a-D neurons, excitation decreases and inhibition increases at higher frequencies. Critically, maximum inhibition is orders of magnitude larger than maximum excitation, suggesting that the timing of inhibition plays a critical role in shaping rhythmic output.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these synaptic characterizations. Reviewer 1 states 'the two types of V2a neurons receive distinct patterns of excitatory and inhibitory inputs during fictive locomotion' and describes the speed-dependent changes in conductances in detail. The observation that inhibition dominates over excitation is implicitly accepted as part of the overall findings on synaptic mechanisms.

results.result: Phase analysis of synaptic currents reveals cell-type-specific and speed-dependent patterns of inhibition. For all V2a neurons, spikes are distributed in-phase with motor output. Phasic excitation in V2a-Ds begins early in anti-phase and precedes that in V2a-Bs, consistent with hierarchical organization. Fast V2a-Ds receive broadly distributed reciprocal (anti-phase) inhibition. Slow V2a-Ds receive two peaks of inhibition: one in-phase (recurrent) and one anti-phase (reciprocal). Fast V2a-Bs receive both in-phase and anti-phase inhibition, while slow V2a-Bs receive predominantly anti-phase inhibition. These patterns suggest that reciprocal inhibition plays a key role in rhythmogenesis at fast speeds, while recurrent inhibition dominates at slow speeds.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support these findings as a major contribution. Reviewer 1 states 'the timing of excitatory and inhibitory inputs was then studied' and describes the phase patterns in detail, noting 'they also show that silencing Dmrt3-labeled dI6 interneurons disrupted rhythm generation selectively at high speed.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes that 'the major claim of the manuscript is well substantiated by Figure 6 and 7' and that 'the authors have done rigorous experiments with statistical analysis to show that reciprocal inhibition is important for rhythmogenesis at fast speeds while recurrent inhibition is key at slow speeds.'

results.result: Synaptic silencing of commissural glycinergic dI6 neurons using botulinum toxin disrupts locomotor rhythmogenesis selectively at high speeds. In dI6 BoTx-GFP fish, synchronous bilateral activity is frequently observed at the beginning of swim episodes (high frequency), which can transition to alternating activity later. Left-right phase values are more broadly distributed in BoTx fish, especially at the beginning of episodes. Below 35 Hz, there are no significant differences in burst frequency or phase between BoTx and control fish, but burst duration and duty cycle are increased. These results indicate that reciprocal inhibition plays a dominant role in rhythm generation at fast speeds and a dominant role in pattern formation at slow speeds.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support these functional experiments as critical validation of the main claims. Reviewer 1 states 'they also show that silencing Dmrt3-labeled dI6 interneurons disrupted rhythm generation selectively at high speed.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes that 'in Figure 7, a specific loss of reciprocal inhibition is shown to disrupt rhythmogenesis at high speeds but not at lower frequencies. These additions in the revised manuscript make the study extremely compelling.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the added dI6 silencing experiments strengthen the claims made regarding the roles of reciprocal inhibition in rhythm and pattern at fast and slow speeds.'

results.result: The main conclusion synthesizes all findings: descending V2a subtypes are recruited exclusively at slow or fast speeds and exhibit intrinsic cellular properties suitable for rhythmogenesis at those speeds, while bifurcating subtypes are recruited more reliably at all speeds and lack appropriate rhythmogenic cellular properties. Phasic firing patterns in both types are shaped by distinct modes of synaptic inhibition linked to cell type and speed. At fast speeds, reciprocal inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing and rhythmogenesis, while recurrent inhibition in bifurcating V2a neurons helps pattern motor output. At slow speeds, recurrent inhibition in descending V2a neurons supports phasic firing and rhythmogenesis, while bifurcating V2a neurons rely on reciprocal inhibition alone to pattern output. These findings suggest cell-type-specific, not common, modes of rhythmogenesis generate and coordinate different speeds of locomotion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously support the main conclusions. The editor states the authors 'present compelling evidence for the diversity in cellular and synaptic properties of one class of spinal interneurons and tie it to their differentiated role in locomotor pattern generation.' Reviewer 1 concludes 'the authors provide compelling evidence that two subtypes of V2as show distinct anatomical, electrophysiological, speed-dependent spiking activity, and receive distinct synaptic inputs as a function of speed' and 'provide an interesting speed-dependent circuit mechanism for rhythm generation.' Reviewer 2 states 'they are able to show that speed related subsets of V2a neurons have distinct cellular and synaptic properties and maybe utilizing different mechanisms to implement different locomotor speeds.' Reviewer 3 affirms 'the overall conclusions are well supported by the data.'

comparisons.comparison: Strong agreement on dI6 silencing experiments (C129-C142). Both evaluations support the finding that dI6 silencing disrupts left-right alternation at high frequencies while maintaining normal frequency at low speeds. Reviewers emphasize this as critical validation of the main claims, with Reviewer 2 calling these additions 'extremely compelling.'

Complete agreement on anatomical distinctions between V2a subtypes (C40-C44). Both evaluations accept the morphological differences in ML position, GFP labeling intensity, and projection patterns. Reviewers explicitly acknowledge these distinctions without critique.

Strong agreement on recruitment patterns (C77-C95). Both evaluations support the differential recruitment of V2a-D and V2a-B neurons across frequency ranges. Reviewers emphasize that identification of V2a subtypes is based directly on their recruitment at different locomotor speeds and praise the physiological relevance of the findings.

Agreement on intrinsic firing properties and their functional relevance (C65-C74). Both evaluations support that V2a-D neurons' intrinsic properties match their recruitment frequencies. Reviewers praise the comparison showing spike rates measured with current steps are physiologically relevant and observed during natural recruitment.

Agreement on electrophysiological characterizations (C55-C64). Both evaluations accept the current-clamp data showing distinct firing patterns. Reviewers praise the 'rigorous approach' and note the authors 'cleverly used standard electrophysiological tests' to distinguish neuronal properties.

Agreement on morphological and basic electrophysiological distinctions (C49-C51). Both evaluations accept these characterizations. Reviewers note the different electrophysiological properties revealed by patch-clamp recordings and praise the rigorous approach of obtaining multiple parameters from the same neuron.

Strong agreement on phase analysis and synaptic timing at fast speeds (C111-C127). Both evaluations support the finding that V2a-D neurons receive excitation earlier than V2a-B neurons and that inhibition timing patterns differ between subtypes. Reviewers emphasize this as a major contribution, with Reviewer 2 stating 'the major claim of the manuscript is well substantiated by Figure 6 and 7.'

Agreement on synaptic current characterizations (C96-C110). Both evaluations accept the voltage-clamp data showing distinct patterns of excitatory and inhibitory inputs. Reviewers accept that the two types of V2a neurons receive distinct patterns of synaptic inputs during fictive locomotion and that inhibition dominates over excitation.

Agreement on speed-dependent inhibition patterns (C116-C128). Both evaluations support the finding that dominant modes of inhibition flip at slow versus fast speeds. Reviewers emphasize that reciprocal inhibition is important for rhythmogenesis at fast speeds while recurrent inhibition is key at slow speeds.

Agreement on normalization of synaptic currents to input resistance (C101-C110). Both evaluations accept the correlations between maximum current and input resistance and that inhibition greatly exceeds excitation, making inhibition timing critical.

Agreement on spike timing and rate data linking intrinsic properties to recruitment (C82-C92). Both evaluations support that spike rates measured with current steps are physiologically relevant and observed during natural recruitment, demonstrating the functional relevance of current-clamp measurements.

Strong agreement on main conclusions (C10, C30, C123-C126, C184). Both evaluations unanimously support the overall conclusions about speed modularity and hierarchical organization. Reviewers provide 'compelling evidence' that V2a subtypes show distinct properties and utilize different mechanisms for different locomotor speeds. The editor affirms the study presents 'compelling evidence for the diversity in cellular and synaptic properties.'

Agreement on hierarchical organization inferences (C114, C119). Both evaluations accept that V2a-D neurons receive excitation earlier than V2a-B neurons, supporting hierarchical organization, and that in-phase inhibition relates to spike coherence.

Agreement on the proposed model (C168, C174-C175). Both evaluations support the comprehensive model integrating experimental findings. Reviewers accept the speed-dependent circuit mechanism for rhythm generation and the overall framework, though it remains a proposed model requiring further testing.

Partial overlap on basic characterization (C52). Both evaluations accept the morphological and electrophysiological distinctions, though they group claims differently. OpenEval focuses on spike timing data while peer review emphasizes the rigorous multi-parameter approach.

Partial overlap on slow speed synaptic patterns (C107-C108). Both evaluations accept the voltage-clamp data at slow speeds, though OpenEval provides more detailed analysis of the phase patterns while peer review accepts the overall finding of speed-dependent synaptic inputs.

Agreement on the surprising finding about synaptic drive (C155). Both evaluations accept that synaptic drive is critical for all V2a neurons, which was surprising given initial hypotheses based on intrinsic properties. This finding is incorporated into the overall supported conclusions.
